dependencies.statement: An admissible polygon in @def-admissible-polygon is stationary when, in a differentiable local chart of its effective vertex coordinates, $DJ(P)[V]=0$ for every vertex variation $V$. On the same chart this is equivalent to $D\lambda_1(P)[V]=0$ for every variation with $DA(P)[V]=0$: the forward implication follows from $DJ=A\,D\lambda_1+\lambda_1\,DA$, and the converse follows by applying the scaling identities $D\lambda_1[X]=-2\lambda_1$ and $DA[X]=2A$ to the radial variation and then using the Lagrange-multiplier decomposition.
dependencies.title: Vertex stationary polygon

target.proof:
By @def-stationary-polygon, the derivative of $J=A\lambda$ vanishes for every vertex displacement. Hadamard's formula is
$$
DJ[V]=A\int_{\partial P}(c-q)V\cdot\nu\,ds.
$$
Moving one endpoint of an effective edge while keeping the other fixed produces an affine normal velocity on that edge, and the two endpoint velocities give the independent functions $1$ and $s/\ell_E$. Since adjacent effective edge normals are linearly independent at a genuine corner, stationarity forces both coefficients of these two affine test functions to vanish. Rescaling $s/\ell_E$ gives the displayed moments.
target.statement:
Let $P$ be admissible and stationary in the sense of @def-stationary-polygon. If $u>0$ is the $L^2$-normalized first eigenfunction, $\lambda=\lambda_1(P)$, $c=\lambda/A(P)$, and $q=|\partial_\nu u|^2$, then every effective edge $E$, parametrized by physical arclength $s\in[0,\ell_E]$, satisfies
$$
\int_E(q-c)\,ds=0,\qquad \int_Es(q-c)\,ds=0.
$$
target.title: Stationary edge moments

gaps: The applicability of the Hadamard formula to polygonal domains under piecewise-affine vertex deformations is invoked without explicitly stating its regularity hypotheses.
The coupled contributions from the two edges incident to a moved vertex are not written as an explicit vector equation; spelling this out would make the use of normal independence fully transparent.
report.repair_hints: State the polygonal Hadamard formula with its hypotheses, and for a vertex variation write the stationarity equation as the sum of the two incident-edge normal vectors multiplied by their respective weighted integrals. Linear independence then gives each coefficient separately.
report.summary: The argument correctly applies the Hadamard shape derivative to vertex variations and uses linear independence of adjacent edge normals to force the two weighted edge moments to vanish, which yields the stated zeroth and first moments.
